message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; if you have a specific dispute, consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What You’re Generally Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|-----------------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent (or two if the lease is for a month‑to‑month tenancy).
• Must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any receipts.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc.).
• Must comply with all applicable building, health, and safety codes. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) of needed repairs.
• If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent, repair & deduct, or pursue a “repair‑and‑deduct” claim in small‑claims court. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if expressly stated in the lease and are reasonable. | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re experiencing hardship. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give at least 24 hours’ notice before entering, except in emergencies.
• Entry is limited to reasonable hours (usually 8 a.m.–10 p.m.). | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord cannot enter without notice, except in emergencies.
• Landlord cannot interfere with your right to quiet enjoyment. | • Report any unlawful entry to the landlord or, if necessary, to the police. | | **Discrimination** | • Protected under the federal Fair Housing Act and Texas Civil Rights Code.
• Discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income is prohibited. | • File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must provide a valid reason for early termination (e.g., breach of lease). | • Provide written notice and keep copies. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a 3‑day notice for non‑payment or lease violation, file a lawsuit, obtain a judgment, and then obtain a writ of possession.
• Eviction cannot be carried out without a court order. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Attend court hearings and bring evidence of compliance. | | **Security Deposit Deductions** | • Landlord may deduct for:
– Unpaid rent
– Damage beyond normal wear & tear
– Cleaning costs if the unit was left dirty
– Replacement of lost keys or locks
– Other costs specified in the lease | • Review the itemized statement.
• Dispute any unjustified deductions in writing. | | **Right to Repair & Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix major problems, you may repair them yourself and deduct the cost from rent, provided you keep receipts and notify the landlord. | • Document the issue, send a written notice, keep receipts, and calculate the deduction. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report disturbances or harassment to the landlord or local authorities. | | **Legal Remedies** | • Small‑claims court (up to $20,000) for disputes over deposits, unpaid rent, or damages.
• Texas Attorney General’s Office or local housing agencies for consumer protection issues. | • File a claim, provide documentation, and attend the hearing. | ### Quick Tips for Protecting Your Rights 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of the lease, receipts, emails, text messages, and photos of the unit’s condition. 2. **Written Communication** – Whenever possible, communicate with your landlord in writing (email or certified mail) so you have a record. 3. **Know the Timeline** – Texas law requires landlords to return security deposits within 30 days of move‑out. If they fail, you can sue for the deposit plus interest. 4. **Seek Mediation First** – Many cities offer free mediation services for landlord‑tenant disputes. This can resolve issues faster than court. 5. **Know Your Local Ordinances** – Some Texas cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas, Houston) have additional tenant protections beyond state law. --- #### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division | Information on tenant rights, how to file complaints | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection | | Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs | Fair housing resources, landlord‑tenant guidelines | https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us/ | | HUD – Fair Housing | Complaint filing, education on discrimination | https://www.hud.gov/program_offices/fair_housing_equal_opp | | Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations | Legal clinics, workshops, advocacy | Search “tenant rights organization Texas” | Feel free to ask if you need more detail on any specific point or help drafting a notice to your landlord!
